items.title: World AIDS Day: People still don’t have access to key HIV prevention medicine

original_payload.original_title: World AIDS Day: People still don’t have access to key HIV prevention medicine
original_payload.original_body:
World
World AIDS Day: People still don’t have access to key HIV prevention medicine
Format
News and Press Release
Source
MSF
Posted
27 Nov 2026
Originally published
27 Nov 2026
Despite generic lenacapavir slowly becoming available for some, Gilead continues to stand in the way of equitable and affordable access amid urgent global need and demand.
NEW YORK/JOHANNESBURG, NOVEMBER 26 —  In advance of World  AIDS  Day on December 1, Doctors Without Borders/Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is once again calling for more people globally to have access to the highly effective HIV prevention medicine  lenacapavir . This twice-yearly injectable version of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is the biggest breakthrough in HIV prevention yet, but US-based Gilead Sciences continues to block affordable access for countries around the world. This includes countries with growing HIV epidemics and ongoing humanitarian crises.
As a result of its long-acting nature, lenacapavir may be especially valuable for stigmatized or criminalized populations, who often are excluded from or concerned about accessing health care. It is also a critical tool for people on the move who may struggle to access health clinics, people living in remote areas with few health care options, and people caught in humanitarian emergencies — including those in many of the communities in which MSF operates.
“Gilead’s greed alone is the reason people across the globe don’t have access to lenacapavir already,” said Carlota Baptista da Silva, MSF’s global HIV/HCV access and advocacy lead. “Our teams are ready to provide it but have been left empty-handed or with very few doses to offer. We have patients in  Eswatini and Zimbabwe  ​ who’ve asked for this medicine and have been told it’s not an option because those countries' stocks had already been depleted. Kenya was supposed to see a priority roll-out but instead has faced severe shortages and delays in access. And communities where the lenacapavir  clinical trials  were held in Brazil, Argentina, Peru, and Mexico haven’t been guaranteed affordable access to it by Gilead.”
A generic version of this twice-yearly PrEP made by Indian manufacturer Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories was  approved  by the US Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) in November. Dr. Reddy’s has agreed to sell its version of lenacapavir for $40 per person per year compared to the more than $28,000 per person per year that Gilead sells it for in the US. The first delivery of generics arrived in Zambia  on the 25th November . However, generics won’t be available everywhere; dozens of middle-income countries will not have access to them because of the restrictive terms of Gilead’s  licensing agreements .
Countries blocked from accessing generics include most of Latin America, where HIV infections  rose 25 percent  between 2010 and 2025. An agreement Gilead has struck with the  Pan American Health Organization (PAHO)  to supply lenacapavir in Latin America does little to ease concerns about access; the agreement ensures Gilead’s total control over supply in the region without revealing the price it will charge. Without the availability of generic lenacapavir, people in these countries are likely to pay far more than the $40 available elsewhere.
“Even with the approval and arrival of generic lenacapavir, Gilead is still dictating which countries can access it and which cannot,” Baptista da Silva said. “The company continues to keep affordable versions of this medicine out of reach for millions by restricting which manufacturers can produce it and where they can sell it. The company could choose to expand the list of countries eligible for affordable generic versions of lenacapavir but is choosing to protect its profits instead. The only way to possibly end AIDS is to increase access to prevention tools like this one."
These access gaps come amid recent funding cuts to HIV programs by many key governments, many of which have historically funded global HIV/AIDS efforts. Prevention efforts and services, particularly those targeting stigmatized populations, have been hit the hardest.
“Many of our patients are caught in conflict, have been forced from their homes, or live in places with few health care options,” Baptista da Silva said. “Only having to get this medicine twice per year would make it much easier for someone to remain protected against HIV even if they’re on the move or unable to access a medical facility between injections. But they can only do that if it’s available more widely and affordable for them. It’s simply unacceptable that a single pharmaceutical company can dictate who can access this medicine and who can’t.”
Lenacapavir must be available for $40 or less in all low- and middle-income countries.  Governments must step in  to help increase access if Gilead continues to block generics from being sold in more countries.
ENDS.

items.title: World AIDS Day 2026 - Statement by Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director of UNAIDS

original_payload.original_title: World AIDS Day 2026 - Statement by Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director of UNAIDS
original_payload.original_body:
World
World AIDS Day 2026 - Statement by Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director of UNAIDS
Format
News and Press Release
Source
UNAIDS
Posted
27 Nov 2026
Originally published
27 Nov 2026
Origin
View original
World AIDS Day 2026 is my last as Executive Director of UNAIDS. Today, we remember the nearly 45 million people we have lost to AIDS and we stand in solidarity with the 41 million people living with HIV and with the communities who have carried this response forward with courage, determination and love.
In reflecting on the past and looking to the future, I feel both immense pride and deep concern.
Pride in what has been achieved through science, solidarity and struggle. Concern that, at the very moment when we have the tools to end AIDS, political choices and deepening inequalities threaten to put that goal beyond our reach.
Thirty years of progress, struggle and solidarity
I remember when an HIV diagnosis was effectively a death sentence. Today, 32.1 million people are receiving life-saving treatment, including 29 million in developing countries.
This extraordinary achievement represents a collective victory. A victory for people living with HIV who refused to accept that their lives were worth less than those of others. For activists who challenged the power of pharmaceutical corporations and held governments to account for realising rights. For communities who confronted prejudice and discrimination. And for governments that recognised their shared responsibility to end a global health crisis.
For decades, the AIDS movement has challenged the inequalities that drive AIDS.
Science must translate into access
Today, science has brought us to another turning point.
Lenacapavir, an HIV prevention injection administered just twice a year, could transform our ability to prevent new infections. By June of this year, more than 50,000 people in nine sub-Saharan African countries had received it. From 2027, generic versions are expected to become available at just US$40 per person per year in eligible lower-income countries. Other long-acting prevention and treatment technologies are advancing rapidly.
Imagine what these innovations could mean for adolescent girls and young women in Africa, who continue to face an unacceptable burden of new HIV infections.
But I have learned one lesson from decades of fighting inequality: a scientific breakthrough is not a public health breakthrough until it reaches the people who need it.
That is why, this World AIDS Day, our message is simple: ending AIDS starts with access.
Access is about rights and justice
Access is about more than the simple existence of a clinic or a treatment. It is about whether medicines are affordable. Whether a person living with HIV can receive treatment without stigma or discrimination Whether a young woman has the power to protect herself. Whether a gay man can seek health care without fear of arrest. Whether a sex worker can enter a clinic without humiliation. Whether activists and communities can organise and gather to protest, demand change, and achieve solidarity.
Access is about power, rights and justice.
And today, all three are under attack.
We cannot allow progress to be reversed
The global AIDS response has been shaken by a financing shock of historic proportions. International HIV assistance fell by 18% in 2025, and the annual financing gap in developing countries now stands at US$4.3 billion.
The latest UNAIDS report reveals the scale of the damage. Across countries reporting data, around 446,000 fewer people received oral HIV prevention medicines in 2025 than in 2024. Worldwide, 300 million fewer condoms were distributed. In priority countries, the number of voluntary medical male circumcisions fell by more than half.
It is unconscionable that, just as science is expanding the possibilities for HIV prevention, access to even the most established prevention tools is being eroded.
And the worst consequences of these cuts still lie ahead. Today's figures cannot yet tell us the full story of the lives that will be affected by the decisions taken over the past two years.
A young woman who fails to access prevention today may acquire HIV tomorrow. A person who loses the support they need to stay on treatment may become seriously ill in the months ahead.
We must act now, before these setbacks translate into needless HIV infections and AIDS-related deaths.
I am particularly concerned about the dismantling of community-led services. Community organisations have been among the first to lose funding, even as organised anti-rights movements are making their work more difficult and, in some places, more dangerous.
These are the organisations that have spent decades building trust with people whom health systems have too often failed. They have reached the most marginalised communities, helped people access prevention and treatment, and defended their right to health.
Once lost, that infrastructure, that knowledge, those relationships and that trust cannot easily be rebuilt.
At the same time, we are witnessing attacks on gender equality, sexual and reproductive health and rights, and the rights of LGBTQ+ people. Civic space is shrinking. Discriminatory laws and policies are driving people away from health services.
We cannot end AIDS while denying people their rights. And we cannot protect the gains of the AIDS response while dismantling the community organisations that made those gains possible.
Countries must have the means to lead
The financing crisis has forced an overdue conversation about the future of the AIDS response. I welcome the growing determination of countries to strengthen national ownership, increase domestic investment and integrate HIV services into inclusive, rights-based national health systems.
UNAIDS has recorded increases in domestic HIV expenditure in 55 countries. Those governments’ leadership deserves recognition and support.
But national ownership cannot mean abandoning international solidarity.
In many countries heavily affected by HIV, debt servicing outstrips public spending on health. This means that scarce revenues are being diverted to pay creditors while organisations are operating on the breadline and individuals are vulnerable.
We cannot expect countries to replace aid financing overnight. And we cannot demand that governments invest more in their people's health while tolerating an international financial architecture that denies them the resources to do so.
We need debt relief and fairer international financing rules. We need a planned transition away from aid, while countries build nationally owned and sustainably financed HIV responses. And we need to reform the rules governing intellectual property so that publicly supported scientific innovation serves the public good, rather than allowing monopolies and high prices to determine who lives and who dies.
These are political choices, driven by interests. But people have confronted interests and changed policies before, and will do again.
We can still end AIDS
Even in this most challenging of years, I have found reasons for hope.
Thirty years ago, UNAIDS was created because the world recognised that defeating AIDS required something different: a joint effort bringing together governments, the United Nations, scientists and communities. That model of solidarity and shared leadership has helped transform the course of the epidemic.
This year, 149 countries voted in favour of an ambitious new United Nations Political Declaration on HIV and AIDS.
Governments committed to reaching 40 million people with HIV treatment and 20 million with antiretroviral-based prevention by 2030. They committed to mobilising US$21.9 billion annually for the AIDS response in low- and middle-income countries, to defending human rights and gender equality, and to strengthening and financing community leadership.
If these commitments are fulfilled, an estimated 3.2 million new HIV infections and 1.3 million AIDS-related deaths could be averted by 2030.
On this World AIDS Day, I urge governments to make HIV a national priority, to invest in sustainable, inclusive and rights-based health systems, to remove the legal and social barriers that deny people access to services, and to ensure that communities are resourced and empowered to lead the AIDS response.
And I urge the international community to renew, rather than retreat from, its commitment to ending AIDS.
As I mark my last World AIDS Day as Executive Director of UNAIDS, I draw strength from the extraordinary courage of the AIDS movement.
Throughout my years leading UNAIDS, I have seen people living with HIV, women's movements, LGBTQ+ activists and other community leaders refuse to surrender, even in the most hostile circumstances. They have defended rights, challenged injustice and kept services alive when institutions failed them.
They remind us that progress is never inevitable. It must be fought for, and protected against backlash or weakening political will.
Ending AIDS requires political courage: to invest in people, defend human rights, confront inequality and put the public good before private profit.
The communities most affected by HIV have shown that courage for decades.
We have the science. We know what works. We know what stands in our way.
The question is no longer whether we can end AIDS. It is whether we will make the choices necessary to do so.
We must not fail this generation.
Ending AIDS starts with access.

items.title: Sudan: El Niño suma nuevos puntos críticos del hambre mientras los conflictos siguen aumentando el riesgo de hambruna, advierten la FAO y WFP

original_payload.original_title: Sudan: El Niño suma nuevos puntos críticos del hambre mientras los conflictos siguen aumentando el riesgo de hambruna, advierten la FAO y WFP
original_payload.original_body:
Sudan
+ 15 more
El Niño suma nuevos puntos críticos del hambre mientras los conflictos siguen aumentando el riesgo de hambruna, advierten la FAO y WFP
Format
News and Press Release
Sources
FAO
WFP
Posted
27 Nov 2026
Originally published
27 Nov 2026
Origin
View original
Sudán, Sudán del Sur, Somalia, algunas zonas de Nigeria y Yemen siguen siendo los puntos críticos de máxima preocupación, mientras que África austral y el Corredor Seco Centroamericano figuran entre las nuevas incorporaciones.
ROMA  – El Niño ha llevado a África austral y al Corredor Seco Centroamericano a la lista de puntos críticos del hambre, donde se prevé que la inseguridad alimentaria aguda empeore significativamente entre diciembre de 2026 y mayo de 2027, advirtieron hoy la Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Alimentación y la Agricultura (FAO) y el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de las Naciones Unidas (WFP). En  su último informe  Hunger Hotspots (Puntos críticos del hambre)  , los organismos también identificaron un riesgo de hambruna en algunas zonas de Sudán y Sudán del Sur.
El informe, publicado dos veces al año a través de la Red Mundial contra las Crisis Alimentarias, identifica 16 puntos críticos, frente a los 13 registrados en junio. El Niño es uno de los principales factores detrás de tres de los cuatro nuevos puntos críticos identificados: África austral (Eswatini, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia y Zimbabwe), el Corredor Seco Centroamericano y el noreste de Uganda. Chad se ha incorporado a la lista debido a los efectos persistentes del conflicto en el vecino Sudán.
El Niño está cobrando fuerza y podría convertirse en uno de los más intensos jamás registrados. En África austral, las condiciones más secas y cálidas amenazan las siembras, las labores agrícolas y las futuras cosechas. Se prevé que hasta 3 millones de personas en Zimbabwe, 2,6 millones en Malawi y 1,8 millones en Mozambique enfrenten altos niveles de inseguridad alimentaria aguda en los próximos meses, hasta marzo de 2027
En el Corredor Seco Centroamericano, la temporada de Primera de 2026 fue la más seca en cuatro décadas y las pérdidas de cultivos superaron el 75 por ciento en muchas zonas. A medida que se agotan las reservas de alimentos, la temporada de escasez de 2027 podría comenzar antes de lo habitual. Solo en Guatemala, se prevé que 3,2 millones de personas enfrenten altos niveles de inseguridad alimentaria aguda entre octubre de 2026 y febrero de 2027.
Actuar antes de que lleguen los peores efectos de El Niño puede evitar daños a las cosechas, el ganado y los medios de vida. El plan conjunto de acción anticipatoria de la FAO y WFP frente a El Niño tiene como objetivo proteger a 9 millones de personas en 22 países.
En otras regiones, los conflictos y la violencia armada siguen figurando entre los principales factores que impulsan la inseguridad alimentaria aguda en 12 de los 16 puntos críticos, incluidos los cinco puntos críticos de máxima preocupación: Sudán, Sudán del Sur, Somalia, algunas zonas de Nigeria y Yemen. En cuatro de estos cinco puntos críticos, los análisis más recientes identificaron o proyectaron poblaciones en situación de Catástrofe, la fase más grave de la Clasificación Integrada de la Seguridad Alimentaria en Fases (CIF), caracterizada por la inanición y la muerte.
En Somalia, aunque actualmente no se prevé que ninguna población enfrente una situación de Catástrofe (Fase 5 de la CIF) y el riesgo de hambruna ha disminuido, la inseguridad alimentaria aguda se mantiene en niveles de Emergencia (Fase 4 de la CIF) entre las poblaciones desplazadas en Baidoa.
Las situaciones más graves se registran en Sudán y Sudán del Sur, donde se ha identificado un riesgo de hambruna. Bajo un escenario razonable de máxima gravedad, existe riesgo de hambruna en 13 zonas de Darfur del Norte y Kordofán del Sur, en Sudán, hasta enero de 2027, mientras que en dos campamentos para personas desplazadas en Darfur del Sur los niveles de malnutrición aguda ya han superado los umbrales de hambruna. En Sudán del Sur, el último análisis disponible indicó un riesgo de hambruna en cuatro condados de los estados de Alto Nilo y Jonglei hasta julio de 2026, bajo un escenario de máxima gravedad.
Los cinco puntos críticos de máxima preocupación se han mantenido reiteradamente en este nivel desde 2022. Sin embargo, la financiación destinada a la asistencia humanitaria para la seguridad alimentaria y la nutrición en estos puntos críticos cayó un 62 por ciento, de USD 5.100 millones en 2022 a USD 2.000 millones en 2025.
Otros cuatro puntos críticos están clasificados como  de muy alta preocupación : Afganistán, la República Democrática del Congo, Haití y Palestina. Aunque la seguridad alimentaria en la Franja de Gaza ha comenzado a mejorar tras el alto el fuego de octubre de 2025, los avances son frágiles y se prevé que la inseguridad alimentaria aguda empeore en Cisjordania.
La FAO y WFP hacen un llamado a adoptar medidas humanitarias urgentes en los 16 puntos críticos, sobre todo allí donde se ha identificado un riesgo de hambruna, y a garantizar un acceso seguro y sin obstáculos a las personas que necesitan asistencia.
“El Niño se está intensificando, amenazando los cultivos y las cosechas en regiones que ya son vulnerables y aumentando el riesgo de inseguridad alimentaria aguda”, afirmó el Director General de la FAO, QU Dongyu. “Sin embargo, los peores escenarios no son inevitables. La asistencia agrícola que salva vidas, destinada a impulsar la producción de alimentos de las familias altamente vulnerables, es una parte esencial de la respuesta multisectorial a las situaciones descritas en el informe. Ahí es donde la FAO está centrando sus esfuerzos”.
“He hecho un llamado a todas las naciones para desterrar la hambruna a los libros de historia”, afirmó el Director Ejecutivo de WFP, Luke J. Lindberg. “Este informe nos indica dónde podría producirse la próxima hambruna, por lo que el momento de cumplir nuestro compromiso es ahora. Será necesario un esfuerzo conjunto para poner fin a los conflictos, dotar de todos los recursos necesarios a nuestros equipos de WFP sobre el terreno y garantizar que tengan acceso seguro para llegar a las comunidades vulnerables. No se trata de un problema de capacidad operativa, sino de si los líderes mundiales tienen el valor político para actuar con decisión”.
# # #
Los 16 puntos críticos del hambre
Máxima preocupación:  Sudán, Sudán del Sur, Somalia, algunas zonas de Nigeria y Yemen.
Muy alta preocupación:  Afganistán, República Democrática del Congo, Haití y Palestina.
Otros puntos críticos:  Chad, Corredor Seco Centroamericano, Madagascar, Malí, Myanmar, África austral (Eswatini, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia y Zimbabwe) y el noreste de Uganda.
Chad, el Corredor Seco Centroamericano, África austral y el noreste de Uganda son nuevas incorporaciones a la lista. Líbano ya no figura como punto crítico.
Nota sobre las fases de la CIF
La Fase 3 de la CIF se refiere a niveles de “Crisis” de inseguridad alimentaria, en los que los hogares presentan brechas en el consumo de alimentos que se reflejan en niveles altos o superiores a los habituales de malnutrición aguda, o apenas pueden satisfacer sus necesidades alimentarias mínimas, pero solo agotando activos esenciales para sus medios de vida o recurriendo a estrategias de afrontamiento de crisis.
La Fase 4 de la CIF se refiere a niveles de “Emergencia” de inseguridad alimentaria, en los que los hogares presentan grandes brechas en el consumo de alimentos, reflejadas en niveles muy altos de malnutrición aguda y exceso de mortalidad, o logran mitigar estas brechas únicamente mediante estrategias de emergencia relacionadas con sus medios de vida y la liquidación de activos.
La Fase 5 de la CIF se refiere a niveles de “Catástrofe/Hambruna”, en los que los hogares enfrentan una carencia extrema de alimentos y/o de otras necesidades básicas incluso después de emplear plenamente sus estrategias de afrontamiento. Son evidentes la inanición, la muerte, la indigencia y niveles extremadamente críticos de malnutrición aguda. A nivel de los hogares, la Fase 5 de la CIF se clasifica como Catástrofe, mientras que la hambruna es una clasificación a nivel de área que requiere pruebas de que se han alcanzado los umbrales de inseguridad alimentaria aguda, malnutrición aguda y mortalidad. El Cadre Harmonisé (CH), utilizado en África Occidental y el Sahel, emplea las mismas fases.
Notas para los editores
Identificados mediante análisis prospectivos, los  puntos críticos del hambre  son zonas donde es probable que la inseguridad alimentaria aguda se deteriore significativamente durante el período de perspectivas. Se seleccionan mediante un proceso basado en el consenso en el que participan los equipos técnicos y sobre el terreno de la FAO y WFP, junto con analistas especializados en conflictos, riesgos económicos y amenazas naturales. El informe se elabora con el apoyo financiero de la Unión Europea a través de la Red Mundial contra las Crisis Alimentarias.
El informe completo puede consultarse  aquí .
El material de apoyo (B-roll) y la lista de tomas pueden consultarse  aquí .
Las fotografías pueden consultarse  aquí .
La Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Alimentación y la Agricultura (FAO) es un organismo especializado que lidera los esfuerzos internacionales para acabar con el hambre. Su objetivo es lograr la seguridad alimentaria para todos y garantizar el acceso regular a suficientes alimentos de alta calidad para llevar una vida activa y saludable. La FAO trabaja en más de 130 países para transformar los sistemas agroalimentarios y hacerlos más eficientes, inclusivos, resilientes y sostenibles.
El Programa Mundial de Alimentos de las Naciones Unidas (WFP) es la organización humanitaria más grande del mundo, que salva vidas en situaciones de emergencia y utiliza la asistencia alimentaria para construir un camino hacia la paz, la estabilidad y la prosperidad para las personas que se recuperan de conflictos, desastres y los efectos de fenómenos meteorológicos extremos

Carte des alertes de maladies épidémiques et émergentes en Océanie - 24 novembre 2026
Format

Source

Éléments nouveaux/faits marquants intervenus depuis la diffusion de la carte précédente sur PacNet, le 17 novembre 2026 :
Maladies diarrhéiques
•  États fédérés de Micronésie (État de Yap) :  D’après le bulletin hebdomadaire de l’État de Yap pour la semaine épidémiologique 46 (du 9 au 15 novembre 2026), le nombre de cas de maladies diarrhéiques a renoué avec le seuil d’alerte (7 cas), après deux semaines sous le seuil : 7 cas ont été signalés dans le service de consultation externe de l’Hôpital de l’État de Yap, contre 3 au cours de la semaine 45. Il s’agissait de 3 enfants âgés de 3 à 5 ans et de 4 adultes âgés de 36 à 64 ans. Sur les deux échantillons de selles testés, l’un s’est révélé positif au rotavirus et l’autre, à  Escherichia coli  entéro-agrégatif. Depuis la semaine 32, le laboratoire a détecté 137 agents pathogènes, essentiellement  E. coli  (59 cas) et le rotavirus (40 cas), avec des co-infections chez 67 % des cas confirmés.  L’alerte bleue pour les maladies diarrhéiques est maintenue pour les États fédérés de Micronésie (État de Yap).   – Source : Département de la santé de Yap, Rapport hebdomadaire sur les maladies transmissibles, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 20 novembre 2026.
Rougeole
•  Papouasie-Nouvelle-Guinée :  Les bulletins hebdomadaires du Département national de la santé pour les semaines épidémiologiques 45 et 46 (du 2 au 15 novembre 2026) font état d’une augmentation du nombre de cas de fièvre éruptive aiguë au niveau national : 11 cas au cours de la semaine 44, 17 au cours de la semaine 45, et 24 au cours de la semaine 46, des chiffres supérieurs à la médiane hebdomadaire habituelle. Au cours de la semaine 46, 16 cas ont été signalés dans la province du Golfe (ils viennent s’ajouter aux deux cas recensés plus tôt dans l’année), ainsi que 3 dans le district de la Capitale nationale, 2 dans les Highlands orientales, 1 à Hela, 1 à Madang et 1 à Manus. Entre le 1er janvier et la semaine 45, 505 cas ont été signalés et 460 échantillons ont été testés, dont 19 se sont révélés positifs aux anticorps IgM de la rougeole. Après examen du groupe d’experts, deux cas de rougeole (1 en Nouvelle-Irlande et 1 dans Highlands occidentales) et deux cas de rubéole restent confirmés en 2026.  L’alerte bleue pour la rougeole est maintenue en Papouasie-Nouvelle-Guinée.   – Source : Département national de la santé de Papouasie-Nouvelle-Guinée, Bulletin hebdomadaire sur les événements de santé publique (semaines épidémiologiques 45 et 46), communiqués au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 20 novembre 2026.
Maladies respiratoires
•  Polynésie française :  La Polynésie française est restée en phase épidémique pour la grippe au cours de la semaine épidémiologique 46 (du 9 au 15 novembre 2026), le nombre de cas confirmés biologiquement passant à 142, dont 139 cas de grippe A. Cinquante-six personnes ont été hospitalisées, dont 7 en réanimation. Deux décès ont été signalés. Depuis le 5 octobre (semaine 41), 427 cas confirmés (dont 372 cas de grippe A), 149 hospitalisations, 13 admissions en réanimation et 6 décès ont été recensés. Le nombre de consultations pour infection respiratoire aiguë au sein du réseau sentinelle reste stable, mais leur proportion augmente. Les autres pathogènes respiratoires détectés sont les suivants : métapneumovirus, parainfluenza 4 et rhino/entérovirus.  L’alerte rouge pour la grippe A est maintenue en Polynésie française.   – Source : Agence de régulation de l’action sanitaire et sociale (ARASS), Bulletin de surveillance sanitaire de Polynésie française no 41, communiqué au point de contact du Groupe de coordination du ROSSP le 24 novembre 2026.
•  Nouvelle-Zélande :  Le rapport hebdomadaire de virologie relatif à la semaine 46 (qui s’est achevée le 15 novembre 2026) fait état de 6 018 prélèvements positifs à la grippe depuis le 1er janvier 2026 : 5 561 cas de grippe A (992 de sous-type A(H1N1)pdm09, 880 de sous-type A(H3N2) et 3 689 non sous-typés) et 457 cas de grippe B. Ce sont 58 cas de plus qu’au cours de la semaine 45, signe que le ralentissement du nombre de détections se poursuit.  L’alerte bleue pour la grippe A est maintenue en Nouvelle-Zélande.   – Source :    PHF Science, Rapport virologique hebdomadaire pour la Nouvelle-Zélande   , page consultée le 24 novembre 2026.
Autres informations :
Entérobactéries productrices de carbapénémase
•  Europe :  Le 18 novembre 2026, le Centre européen de prévention et de contrôle des maladies (ECDC) a indiqué que l’incidence estimée des infections sanguines à  Klebsiella pneumoniae , une bactérie productrice de carbapénémase, avait atteint 3,75 pour 100 000 habitants en 2025 dans l’Union européenne/Espace économique européen (UE/EEE). Ce taux est supérieur de 72 % au niveau de référence de 2019 et dépasse largement l’objectif 2030 (2,07 pour 100 000 habitants). L’ECDC estime que le risque est très élevé pour les personnes recevant des soins médicaux dans l’UE/EEE. La circulation de bactéries hébergeant l’enzyme New Delhi métallo-β-lactamase (NDM) augmente, avec au moins un isolat positif dans 84,3 % des territoires en 2025 contre 44,7 % en 2019 ; les détections d’ E. coli  producteurs de carbapénémase sont de plus en plus fréquentes en milieu communautaire. Les infections sanguines dues à des souches d’ E. coli  résistantes aux céphalosporines de troisième génération ont augmenté de 16,4 %, et seuls cinq pays ont atteint leurs objectifs nationaux en 2025.  – Source :    BEACON, EU/EEA : Rising carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae and E. coli bloodstream infections threaten 2030 AMR targets    et    Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales - fourth update   , pages consultées le 24 novembre 2026.
Diphtérie
•  Australie :  Le point de situation national daté du 16 novembre 2026 fait état de 653 cas de diphtérie signalés en 2026, dont un cas probable, contre une moyenne de 17 cas pour la même période entre 2022 et 2025. Quatorze cas ont été signalés au cours de la dernière quinzaine, contre 12 au cours de la quinzaine précédente : 7 en Australie-Occidentale, 5 dans le Territoire du Nord, 1 en Australie-Méridionale et 1 dans le Queensland, dont 4 cas de diphtérie respiratoire. L’activité reste inférieure au pic intervenu entre fin mai et début juin 2026. Depuis le 1er janvier, des cas ont été recensés dans le Territoire du Nord (336), en Australie-Occidentale (287), en Australie-Méridionale (24) et dans le Queensland (6) ; tous les cas autochtones appartiennent au même groupe génomique. Les Aborigènes et/ou les Insulaires du détroit de Torres représentent 95,3 % des cas, et 88,9 % des cas autochtones vivent dans des zones reculées ou très reculées. Deux tiers des cas (66,3 %) sont cutanés et 30,8 % sont respiratoires. Au total, 120 personnes (18,4 % des cas) ont été hospitalisées et un décès a été signalé en avril 2026.  – Source :    Australian Centre for Disease Control, Diphtheria in Australia, epidemiological update as at 16 November 2026   , page consultée le 24 novembre 2026.
Maladies respiratoires
•  Monde :  Le 19 novembre 2026, le Groupe consultatif technique sur l’évolution du virus SARS-CoV-2 (TAG-VE) de l’Organisation mondiale de la Santé (OMS) a qualifié le variant PJ.2.1 du SARS-CoV-2 de « variant sous surveillance », indiquant que le risque supplémentaire pour la santé publique était faible au niveau mondial. Issu de la lignée JN.1, ce variant a été détecté pour la première fois dans la province canadienne de l’Ontario, en mai 2026. Il a ensuite progressé, passant de 1,0 % des séquences analysées au cours de la semaine 33 à 11,6 % au cours de la semaine 41. Ces pourcentages ont été établis sur la base de 722 séquences transmises par 18 pays au 8 novembre 2026. L’OMS signale également la remontée de signaux de surveillance des eaux usées pouvant témoigner d’une circulation communautaire en Nouvelle-Zélande et à Hong Kong. Les anticorps induits par les vaccins actuels restent capables de neutraliser ce variant.  – Source :    BEACON, SARS-CoV-2 variant PJ.2.1 spreads globally via enhanced ACE2 binding while current vaccine antibodies retain neutralization    et    WHO TAG-VE Risk Evaluation for SARS-CoV-2 Variant Under Monitoring   , pages consultées le 24 novembre 2026.

items.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths

original_payload.original_title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
original_payload.original_body:
Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
Image source,  Reuters
Image caption,    The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves
By  Patrick Jackson
Published
27 November 2026, 16:06 GMT
Updated 1 hour ago
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.
Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.
Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.
Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.
The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.
Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.
The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.
"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.
The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".
Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.
Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.
The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.
Earlier this week, Mackenzie was also convicted of:
assault causing actual bodily harm and five counts of cruelty to a child
engaging in organised criminal activity
radicalisation
facilitating the commission of a terrorist act
being in possession of an article connected with an offence under Kenya's Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2012.
Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders
Published
19 October
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.
A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
After the main church shut down in 2019, Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest.
"We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," said survivor Peter Shukrani, who was rescued after falling ill.
Image source,  Mohamed Madi / BBC
Image caption,    Stephen Mwiti, who lost six children to the cult, welcomed the conviction of Mackenzie for murder last month
When the shallow graves were discovered, local men were hired for the horrifying task of exhuming the remains.
"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."
"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."
Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".
Post-mortem records showed many of the victims had died of starvation while the remains of others were mostly skeletal, making the establishment of their cause of death impossible.
Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he had lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.
"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court last month.
"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest. I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."
The deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.
Additional reporting by Thomas Mukhwana

items.title: Ex-Kenyan governor jailed for 25 years over pregnant girlfriend's murder

original_payload.original_title: Ex-Kenyan governor jailed for 25 years over pregnant girlfriend's murder
original_payload.original_body:
Ex-Kenyan governor jailed for 25 years over pregnant girlfriend's murder
Image source,  Reuters
Image caption,    It is rare for such a high-ranking official to face public criminal trials in Kenya
By  Basma El Atti    Reporting from Nairobi
Published
27 November 2026, 11:16 GMT
Updated 7 hours ago
A former Kenyan governor has been jailed for 25 years for the murder of a university student who was seven months pregnant with his child.
The High Court on Friday sentenced Zacharia Okoth Obado, the former governor of Migori County, along with two former aides, over the 2018 killing of Sharon Belyne Otieno.
The investigation established that an "intimate relationship" had existed between Obado and Otieno, which "subsequently led to a pregnancy with the deceased that the governor was unhappy about".
Both Obado and Otieno's legal teams said they would appeal against the sentence.
His former personal assistant, Michael Oyamo, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison, while former county clerk Caspal Ojwang' Obiero received an 18-year sentence.
The court found that Obado had provided the motive and financial resources for the murder, while Oyamo coordinated its execution and Obiero provided logistical support and helped conceal the crime.
Judge Cecilia Githua said Obado's absence from Migori at the time of the killing did not absolve him of responsibility.
She rejected the prosecution's request for the death penalty, as well as Obado's plea for a non-custodial sentence.
Otieno, 26, was killed between 3 and 4 September 2018 after leaving a hotel in Rongo, south-western Kenya, with journalist Barrack Oduor.
She had contacted Oduor to discuss her relationship with the then-governor. The two were abducted shortly afterwards.
Oduor managed to escape by jumping out of a moving vehicle. His account of the abduction became a crucial lead in the investigation.
Otieno's body was later found near Kodera Forest.
A post-mortem examination found that she had died from strangulation and excessive bleeding caused by multiple stab wounds.
The court also established that Obado was the biological father of her unborn child.
Obado and his co-accused were convicted of murder on 23 July 2026, following a lengthy trial in which prosecutors called 42 witnesses and presented 81 exhibits.
On Friday, the court declined to award compensation to Otieno's family, saying there was insufficient evidence to establish the financial losses they had claimed.
Before sentencing, Otieno's mother had appealed to the judge not to send Obado to prison, saying his imprisonment would amount to "another death in the family".
She urged the court to consider a non-custodial sentence, arguing that Otieno's three children, from different relationships, needed his support.
But the judge said the family's circumstances could not override the court's responsibility to impose an appropriate punishment.
Otieno's family, through their lawyer Antony Opondo, told Kenya's Daily Nation that they would file an appeal seeking Obado's acquittal.
Otieno's murder sparked protests and renewed public debate about violence against women in Kenya.
A national survey found that at least 34% of women had experienced physical violence in 2022.
The case has also drawn attention because it is rare for such senior political figures to face public criminal trials in Kenya.
Obado served two terms as governor of Migori County in western Kenya, switching allegiance between a smaller political party and the region's dominant opposition movement.
He later backed President William Ruto and formally joined his ruling party in 2023, becoming a regional organiser.

items.title: Uganda to withdraw troops from DR Congo town amid diplomatic row

original_payload.original_title: Uganda to withdraw troops from DR Congo town amid diplomatic row
original_payload.original_body:
Uganda to withdraw troops from DR Congo town amid diplomatic row
Image source,  AFP via Getty Images
Image caption,    The planned withdrawal will end Uganda's nearly two-year campaign against ADF militants in Lubero
By  Wycliffe Muia
Published
8 hours ago
Uganda has announced plans to withdraw its troops from a town in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo within two weeks, as diplomatic tensions escalate between the two neighbours.
The troops will hand over security in Lubero, in North Kivu province, to Congolese forces after nearly two years of military operations, the Ugandan army said in a statement on Friday.
The announcement comes days after  DR Congo summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over controversial social media posts  by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is the son of President Yoweri Museveni.
The Ugandan military did not give a reason for the withdrawal or say whether it was linked to the diplomatic row.
What are Ugandan forces doing in DR Congo?
The Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) were deployed to Lubero to pursue fighters from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) Islamist group fleeing joint military operations elsewhere in eastern DR Congo.
The ADF, which originated in Uganda in the 1990s, is affiliated to the Islamic State and has been blamed for numerous deadly attacks on civilians in both countries.
Uganda first deployed troops to eastern DR Congo under the current joint military campaign in November 2021, following a series of bomb attacks in the Ugandan capital, Kampala.
Ugandan army spokesperson Col Chris Magezi said that the joint military campaign, known as Operation Shujaa, would continue elsewhere in DR Congo.
The planned withdrawal applies only to Lubero town.
Five years into the joint offensive, the ADF remains DR Congo's deadliest armed group, despite a significant decline in its activities in Uganda, according to the conflict monitoring organisation Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (Acled).
John Ngono, Acled's DR Congo analyst, said the group was killing an average of four civilians a day and had expanded into previously unaffected parts of eastern DR Congo.
He said the findings suggested that "Operation Shujaa may have improved security in Uganda while shifting the geographical impact of violence within the DRC".
Acled says the group has not carried out an attack in Uganda since June 2025, but its growing interest in mineral resources in DR Congo could help finance its operations and sustain its ability to threaten both countries.
The planned withdrawal comes amid strained relations between Uganda and DR Congo, despite years of close military co-operation.
Earlier this week, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to endorse a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo, threatening that Ugandan troops would seize it themselves if the rebels failed to do so.
The Congolese foreign ministry described his remarks as "particularly serious" and demanded that Uganda clarify its official position and take steps to prevent similar incidents.
Gen Kainerugaba also defended Uganda's military presence in eastern DR Congo, insisting it was driven by security concerns.
The planned withdrawal comes amid renewed fighting between Congolese forces and rebels in the wider Lubero territory, raising fresh concerns about the safety of civilians.
Eastern DR Congo has endured decades of conflict involving dozens of armed groups, with millions of people forced to flee their homes.

items.title: UK police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly convicted over attack on British couple

original_payload.original_title: UK police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly convicted over attack on British couple
original_payload.original_body:
Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly convicted over attack on UK couple
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be played
Figure caption,    Watch: Man wrongly sentenced to death says Met Police ruined his life
By  Jean Mackenzie    Reporting from Lamu
Published
27 November 2026, 00:48 GMT
A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly convicted and sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.
Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.
Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.
Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.
In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.
We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.
It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.
Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.
"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.
Image source,  Judith Tebbutt
Image caption,    David and Judith Tebbutt were on a dream holiday to Kenya when they were attacked
Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.
"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."
Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.
"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."
Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.
"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".
The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.
Image caption,    Ali Kololo says he lost contact with his children while he was in prison
Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.
But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.
In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.
The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the  Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks .
At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.
"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.
Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".
"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."
Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.
Image source,  shutterstock
Image caption,    Neil Hibberd retired from the police in 2017
In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction,  because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence . This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.
They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.
"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."
More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."
He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.
Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.
"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."
He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.
"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."
For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.
"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."
The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.
"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.
The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."
Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".
"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."
"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."
Additional reporting by Ed Habershon

items.title: Guinea-Bissau's military leaders delay return to civilian rule until 2028

original_payload.original_title: Guinea-Bissau's military leaders delay return to civilian rule until 2028
original_payload.original_body:
Guinea-Bissau's military leaders delay return to civilian rule until 2028
Image source,  Getty Images
Image caption,    Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam said the postponement was driven by factors including final reasons
By  Simi Jolaoso   Africa correspondent
Published
9 hours ago
Guinea-Bissau's military rulers have postponed elections scheduled for next week by two years, delaying the return to civilian rule.
Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam announced in a decree that the presidential and parliamentary elections, originally due on 6 December, would now take place on 26 November 2028.
The announcement came exactly a year after the military seized power, promising to return the country to civilian rule within 12 months.
In a statement, the presidency said an assessment of electoral preparations had found that there were insufficient "technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the polls as planned.
It said the delay would provide more time to ensure the elections were credible, transparent and inclusive, with all candidates given equal opportunities.
The presidency also reiterated its commitment to holding the country's first-ever local government elections but gave no date for the vote.
Gen N'Tam was sworn in as transitional president a day after the military overthrew President Umaro Sissoco Embaló in November 2025.
The coup took place three days after general elections and a day before provisional results were due to be announced.
Both Embaló and his main challenger, Fernando Dias, had claimed victory.
Embaló, who has since been living in exile in Morocco, was barred from returning to Guinea-Bissau last month, despite expressing an interest in contesting the elections.
Guinea-Bissau has experienced several coups and attempted coups since gaining independence from Portugal in 1974.

items.title: Mali: Mali Remains Strategic for Russia Despite Heavy Losses, Investigator Says

original_payload.original_title: Mali: Mali Remains Strategic for Russia Despite Heavy Losses, Investigator Says
original_payload.original_body:
Russia is unlikely to pull out of Mali despite losing more than 10 percent of its forces there, an investigator who tracks Russian military deployments told RFI. Lou Osbourn co-founded All Eyes On Wagner, a collective of journalists and cybersecurity analysts. She said the losses prove that Russian fighters are taking part in operations alongside Malian troops and that "Africa remains an area of interest for Moscow".
The United Kingdom's  The Guardian  newspaper - which had access to the leaked records through a media consortium that includes RFI -  reported on Tuesday  that 349 Russian fighters were killed in  Mali  between September 2023 and September 2026.
It based its tally on death certificates held by Russia's national statistics agency, Rosstat, but said that the real figure was probably higher because deaths can take time to be registered.

items.title: Southern Africa: Crowded Waters - Can Southern Africa Steer Mozambique Channel Security?

original_payload.original_title: Southern Africa: Crowded Waters - Can Southern Africa Steer Mozambique Channel Security?
original_payload.original_body:
Rising international interest and insurgent activity at sea should push regional states to reassess their maritime commitments and capabilities.
Visits to Mozambique and Madagascar in November by Lieutenant General John Brennan, Deputy Commander of United States (US) Africa Command (AFRICOM), underscore the Mozambique Channel's growing strategic weight.
Alongside the channel's significance as a global commercial shipping route, AFRICOM  highlighted  Islamic State Mozambique's (ISM) developing maritime capabilities and the security of Cabo Delgado's multibillion-dollar onshore and offshore liquefied natural gas (LNG) investments.

items.title: Eritrea: Eritrea Accuses Ethiopia of Using Maritime Diplomacy to 'Camouflage Its Irredentist Ambitions'

original_payload.original_title: Eritrea: Eritrea Accuses Ethiopia of Using Maritime Diplomacy to 'Camouflage Its Irredentist Ambitions'
original_payload.original_body:
Addis Abeba — Eritrea has accused Ethiopia of using maritime diplomacy and regional security forums to mask what it described as territorial ambitions in the Horn of Africa, escalating tensions amid renewed disagreements over Ethiopia's pursuit of Red Sea access.
In a statement issued Thursday, Eritrea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused the Prosperity Party government of seeking to "manufacture a veneer of international legitimacy" around its demand for "sovereign sea access," which Asmara characterized as territorial revisionism.
The statement follows Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's address to the House of Peoples' Representatives on Thursday, November 26, in which  he rejected claims that Ethiopia intends to invade Eritrea , but reiterated that access to the Red Sea remains a strategic imperative to be pursued through dialogue.

items.title: Ghana: Why Ghana Is Moving to Protect Its Traditional Palm Spirit and What It Could Mean for Producers, Consumers and the Country's Global Reputation

original_payload.original_title: Ghana: Why Ghana Is Moving to Protect Its Traditional Palm Spirit and What It Could Mean for Producers, Consumers and the Country's Global Reputation
original_payload.original_body:
GHANA is on the verge of doing for Apio what Scotland did for Scotch Whisky and what France did for Cognac. Across the world, some of the most successful products are not simply commodities. They are products whose value is inseparable from the places, traditions and communities that produce them.
The country's traditional palm-based spirit, distilled exclusively from fermented palm sap, is deeply rooted in local knowledge, rural livelihoods and cultural identity. Through the development of a Geographical Indication (GI), Ghana now has an opportunity not only to preserve this heritage but also to transform it into a source of long-term economic value.
A geographical indication identifies products whose qualities, reputation or characteristics are linked to a specific place of origin. Around the world, GI protection has helped transform local products into globally recognised brands while protecting producers from imitation and misuse.

An aide to the Delta governor resigned over campaign killings as INEC named nine states affected by political attacks. Seyi Makinde's campaign denied plans to withdraw for Atiku Abubakar, who challenged the APC's claims on housing delivery and job creation.
The political fallout from Monday's deadly political violence in Delta State widened with the resignation of Tonia Gbemre, an aide to Governor Sheriff Oborevwori, as the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) identified nine states where political attacks have occurred since open campaigns began in August.
While National Security Adviser Nuhu Ribadu pledged impartial protection for political actors and voters, efforts to build a common opposition front faced a fresh test as Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde's campaign denied plans to withdraw in favour of former Vice President Atiku Abubakar. items.title: Liberia: 'No Perfect Concession, but Liberia Needs Power and Roads'

original_payload.original_title: Liberia: 'No Perfect Concession, but Liberia Needs Power and Roads'
original_payload.original_body:
Deputy Speaker Thomas P. Fallah has thrown his weight behind the government's $5.7 billion Master Infrastructure Development Agreement (MIDA), calling it laudable and necessary for Liberia's development, but insisting the Legislature will fully scrutinize the document before any vote.
Speaking in an interview on Thursday, Fallah said the deal, which focuses on electricity and road infrastructure, comes at a critical moment for the country, even though it has not yet reached the Legislature.
"For me as a person, I think it's something that is laudable because given the history of our country, our road network and road connectivity has been one of our major challenges," Fallah said. "The issue of power, electricity, cannot be overemphasized."

items.title: Liberia: Former VP Howard-Taylor Seeks Recusal of Trial Judge

original_payload.original_title: Liberia: Former VP Howard-Taylor Seeks Recusal of Trial Judge
original_payload.original_body:
Former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor has asked Criminal Court 'C' Judge Ousman F. Feika to recuse himself from Liberia's US$317 million cocaine trafficking case, alleging that remarks he made about her have raised serious questions about his impartiality and her constitutional right to be presumed innocent.
In a motion filed Wednesday, November 25, Howard-Taylor's lawyers requested that Judge Feika withdraw from the proceedings, suspend all further action in the case and have it reassigned to another judge.
The defence argues that the judge's alleged description of Howard-Taylor as a "criminal defendant" before the determination of the charges creates the appearance that he has prejudged her guilt, undermining confidence in the fairness of the trial.

Local Government Minister Ben Phiri has told a national conference that Malawi's economic troubles were decades in the making, and that everyone must share the blame.
Speaking at the fifth National Conference on Public Debt, Taxation and Climate Finance in Lilongwe, Phiri said: "All of us must be ashamed. The road to where we are today did not start yesterday. The road to where we started a long time ago, and most of us share the blame."

He also called for more domestic production, industrialisation, value addition and exports to tackle the country's chronic forex shortages.

items.title: Mozambique: Banning a Film of People Saying They Are Powerless Stresses What They Are Saying

original_payload.original_title: Mozambique: Banning a Film of People Saying They Are Powerless Stresses What They Are Saying
original_payload.original_body:
The treason trial of Venancio Mondlane is claiming to ask who is responsible for the violence in the post-election demonstrations. The answer from ordinary people filmed in demonstrations and interviews is in the banned OMR film “Isn’t this our country?” (Nao e nosso pais este aqui?) The 45 minute film is particularly good in recording both the power people felt in the demonstrations, their disempowerment facing the damage done to their lives by mining, and the powerlessness faced by young people with no jobs and no future.
The powerlessness was stressed by the 9 October 2024 general elections, with widespread fraud. (I was in Maputo reporting that election for CIP, and the fraud was so great no one knows who actually won.) Ten days later, on 19 October, Elvino Dias, the official lawyer for opposition candidate Venancio Mondlane, was gunned down in Maputo. On 21 October Mondlane held a press conference at the site of the murder, calling for protests, and he and the journalists were teargassed by the police. That propelled the demonstrations, but in protests from 21 to 25 October police killed 24 people. That created a wave of anger, and demonstrations took on a different tone. The film shows that the response was attacks on symbols of party and state power – burning Frelimo offices and police stations.

items.title: Africa: AfDB and Ebrd Set Out a Shared Vision for a Stronger Partnership Across Africa

original_payload.original_title: Africa: AfDB and Ebrd Set Out a Shared Vision for a Stronger Partnership Across Africa
original_payload.original_body:
Leaders of the African Development Bank Group (AfDB) and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) met in Abidjan on Tuesday 24 November to set out a shared vision for the next phase of their well-established partnership, building on their complementary strengths and broader shared footprint across Africa.
A day after the EBRD opened its country office in Abidjan, African Development Bank Group President Sidi Ould Tah and EBRD President Odile Renaud-Basso held a fireside conversation with staff of the two institutions on financing businesses, expanding access to energy, and the role African savings can play in these investments.
Earlier in the day, the two presidents opened the Africa Small and Medium Enterprise Business Day at the Noom Hotel, attended by some 200 leaders of financial institutions, investors and business executives. The president of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU) Commission, Abdoulaye Diop, and Côte d'Ivoire's Minister of Commerce, Industry and Crafts, Kalil Konaté, also addressed the gathering. The goal of the day: to build a coalition for African SMEs.
The discussions focused on tackling practical barriers holding back African SMEs. For instance, an SME that wins an order from a large manufacturer must finance its purchases and production before it gets paid. A guarantee can help it obtain credit, but this only works if the company keeps reliable accounts and has a market for its products. Financing alone is not enough and supporting SMEs through tailored advisory is also very important to guarantee success.
Mid-sized companies are the least well served: too large for schemes designed for small businesses yet not structured enough to convince major financiers. Development banks, commercial banks, guarantee funds, and investors are therefore being urged to share risks more effectively and to coordinate their support according to each company's stage of growth.
The morning also covered SMEs' access to regional and international markets and their place in the supply chains of large industrial groups. The approach builds on the Bank's SME Development Action Plan 2026-2031, which combines financing, technical assistance and access to markets and has identified supply chain financing as an important priority.
In the afternoon, in a fireside conversation with AfDB staff gathered at the Bank's headquarters in Abidjan and EBRD staff joining online, the two presidents highlighted the complementary strengths of their institutions. AfDB brings deep continental knowledge and presence, strong government relationships, public-sector financing and convening power, while EBRD brings a predominantly private-sector model, together with experience in policy and regulatory reform, market development and mobilising private capital. As the two institutions operate in more common markets, they committed to deepen practical cooperation where it can add value for clients and markets.
For instance, the two banks are jointly working on a project called EnterpRise Africa. It would target fast-growing SMEs ready to scale up, but struggling to identify credit solutions that are modelled around their growth trajectories and business specificities.
The project has two components: a private credit fund, and an advisory platform to help these businesses strengthen their management, governance, and ability to raise additional capital.
Nine countries are being considered: Benin, Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria and Senegal, where both banks operate, as well as Burkina Faso, Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo, three Transition States where the AfDB would operate alone.
original_payload.original_summary: [African Development Bank (AfDB)] Leaders of the African Development Bank Group (AfDB) and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) met in Abidjan on Tuesday 24 November to set out a shared vision for the next phase of their well-established partnership, building on their complementary strengths and broader shared footprint across Africa.

items.title: Armed men kill 13 guards in 'terrorist attack' in western Niger

original_payload.original_title: Armed men kill 13 guards in 'terrorist attack' in western Niger
original_payload.original_body:
Niger
Armed men on Thursday killed at least 13 Nigerien guards in an attack in the restive Tillaberi region in western Niger, the defence ministry said in a statement.
The Nigerien National Guard was targeted  "by a terrorist attack carried out by a large group of heavily armed assailants,"  the ministry said in a statement read on public television.
Niger, ruled by a military junta since a 2023 coup, is battling violence by jihadists linked to Al-Qaeda and the Islamic State group, with thousands killed over the last decade.
